description_full: MBRF Global Foods Company S.A., through its subsidiaries, operates in the food industry in Brazil and internationally. It operates through Beef North America, Beef South America, and BRF segments. The company produces, processes, distributes, and sells animal-based proteins, such as beef, pork, lamb, fish, and poultry; pasta, margarine, vegetable, pet food, and plant-based proteins; processed hamburgers; and various ready-to-eat products. It also engages in leather industrialization; trading activities; transportation; transportation leasing; energy generation, trading, and related services; processing, sale, distribution, and retail of animal feed and nutritional products; road freight; manufacture, distribution, and marketing of pet food products; and processing of canned meats and other processed products. In addition, the company provides administrative and marketing services, logistics services, and consulting services. It imports, sells, and exports its products to restaurant and supermarket chains, and homes. The company sells its products under the Sadia, Sadia Bassi, Perdigão, Perdigão Montana, Perdigão Na Brasa, Qualy, Claybom, Deline, Banvit, Paty, and Quickfood brands. MBRF Global Foods Company S.A. was founded in 1986 and is headquartered in São Paulo, Brazil.

financial_summary: Marfrig Global Foods SA is a mid-cap consumer defensive business with a $4.0B market cap on $29.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +6% over the past three years, a respectable pace for a business of this size.

Returns on capital run at 10% against a 10% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically, and 13% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $1.4B in free cash flow — roughly 5 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 36.51× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -9.0% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 4.0× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and thin 0.8× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 26.8% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.4× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.
